data.title: Asia Markets, Tech Firms Sink on AI Fears; Cyberattacks on Japan
data.description:
Sharemarkets in Japan and Korea were hit hard on Friday after the plunge on Wall Street overnight, spurred by fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress will ramp up regulation on data centres and the AI sector.

The Nikkei in Tokyo fell by 5.96% and the Kospi in Seoul dropped by 6.02%. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong was down 1.27%, while Shanghai was down 1.1%.

While the historic “blue wave” in mid-term voting on Tuesday was welcomed initially on hopes it could pressure President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, but fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore.

 

ALSO SEE: China’s ‘Bipolar’ Economy; Possible 3-Heads Summit in Shenzhen

 

Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.

Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.

The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.

The dramatic rally in many companies’ valuations had also caused unease on trading floors.

Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights said investors were selling up because of “concerns that we might see greater opposition to AI buildout plans, with the results in Texas prompting concerns that politicians in the state might target Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX due to his support for Trump”.

The Nasdaq in New York plunged 5.5% in its worst day – percentage-wise – since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. The S&P 500 tanked more than 4% and the Dow more than 3%.

Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16% this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.

Trump blamed the collapse on the Democrats, writing on Truth Social: “The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!”

 

Kospi down nearly 50% since June

The heavy selling continued in Asia.

Seoul briefly plunged almost 9% before ending 6% lower with chip giant SK Hynix off more than 10% while rival Samsung was 6.4% down.

The Kospi rose by over 75% last year and more than doubled between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, and has lost almost 50% since then.

In Tokyo, SoftBank gave back more than 10%, with Kioxia off 8.7% and Advantest 5% lower.

In Taiwan, TSMC dropped 4.7%, which dragged the Taiex down about the same.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Jakarta, Bangkok, Wellington and Manila were also in the red.

Meanwhile, London, Paris and Frankfurt all fell more than 1% when they opened.

Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets said: “The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre buildout… this looks totally overdone, but the nature of sell-everything of this market means we need to look for some stability first.”

The mood was also dampened by a rise in oil prices, extending Thursday’s gains after plunging on the mid-term results amid hopes for an end to the Iran war.

Traders were keeping eyes on developments in the crisis after US and Iranian leaders had indicated progress earlier in the week.

US jobs data is also due later in the day, following broadly positive readings earlier in the week.

 

Japan responds to cyberattacks

There was plenty of other news in Asia on Friday. First, Japan is set to announce the launch of a “cyber rescue team” later today in response to a sudden wave of hacking incidents.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to compile an emergency package of measures after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.

Hacks and data breaches have ballooned worldwide, with AI’s ability to find previously unknown ways to break into computer systems in the global spotlight.

Takaichi’s office confirmed her cabinet will hold a ministerial meeting on cybersecurity on Friday.

The policy package will include the creation of a “cyber rescue team” made up of both government and private sector experts, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily, Jiji Press and other media reported.

The government will set up a secretariat within the current fiscal year to coordinate the deployment of the rescue team when support needs are particularly acute, the reports said.

A “Top Gun Talent Team” of specialists will also be deployed this month to simulate attacks in a push to boost security, Jiji Press reported.

The measures will be “the first step towards transitioning to a society that meets the world’s top standards of cyber resilience”, top government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters on Thursday.

The package will be “one that prevents damage from occurring as much as possible, and, if damage does occur, is able to respond immediately”, he said.

Chinese artificial intelligence cybersecurity tool Artex was used in several recent hacks of Japanese companies, an information security arm of Japanese IT firm GMO Internet Group said last month. GMO Internet Group is among those that have come under attack.

 

Protest over Moscow seizing Japan Tobacco assets

Meanwhile, Tokyo lodged a protest with Moscow demanding the immediate release of Japan Tobacco’s assets that were seized by the Kremlin, government spokesman Minoru Kihara said on Friday.

Kihara said two Japanese senior officials visiting Russia “had lodged a protest with the Russian government together with the ambassador of Japan to Russia, and demanded the immediate withdrawal of the measure”.

data.title: China’s ‘Bipolar’ Economy; Possible 3-Heads Summit in Shenzhen
data.description:
A former senior official at the IMF noted last week that China appears to have an extraordinary ‘boom and gloom’ economy – a country with two very different sides.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, said that while China’s export industries such as EVs, solar panels and many manufactured goods are “the envy of the world”, the country’s growth is “deeply unbalanced.”

While its tech and AI industries are topped only by the United States, the rest of its economy is stuck in the sixth year of a “full-blown, Japan-style real estate crisis,” which has left domestic consumption stagnating in the doldrums.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Stocks Rise; Dollar Down on Democrats’ Electoral Sweep

 

Part of the country’s problem is that its dynamic sectors, such as robotics and AI, are not creating enough jobs, which means the country’s youth unemployment problem is so bad that Beijing no longer publishes the figures regularly.

Because China is not a democracy, it is possible, he said, that 450 million people are part of the most dynamic sectors that are currently thriving, while more than double that number – another 950 million citizens – have to survive on a “much lower” standard of living, despite the fact President Xi’s regime has sought to ease regional disparities since he came to power in 2013.

Wealth inequality is a problem that plagues countries all over the world, including America.

Rogoff, a former professor of economics and public policy at Harvard and an author of multiple books, who is 73 now, said that China’s excessive construction is likely to “hold down growth for years to come.”

But he suggested the dynamic core of its industrial sector should continue to thrive, as long as it remains politically stable – and doesn’t fall for “temptations of imperial overreach.”

There was no mention of Taiwan. All the indicators and reports we’ve seen in recent years suggest Rogoff is right on the money. His latest report can be read here.

 

Three leaders to meet?

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump appears to have taken the battering endured by his Republican allies in the mid-term elections this week in relatively subdued fashion.

Washington is alive with speculation on how the ‘blue wave’ that has dramatically changed the country’s political scene will play out.

Beijing is still eager to lure the US leader to the APEC summit it will hold in Shenzhen this month – and it’s possible that Trump has bigger things in mind than his party’s electoral drubbing.

China said on Wednesday it was in contact with the United States and Russia about a possible three-way leaders’ meeting on the sidelines of the regional gathering in Shenzhen in a couple of weeks time.

“China is in communication on a China-Russia-US heads of state meeting with relevant parties,” foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular briefing when asked about the possible trilateral summit on the sidelines of the APEC meeting on November 18-19, AFP reported.

The Kremlin said on October 21 that the meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin – which would be a first – was “being prepared”.

Xi, 73, and Trump, 80, have already met twice this year – most recently with the Chinese leader visiting the White House in September – and they are due to come together again at a G20 summit in Miami in December.

The two leaders vowed to extend a trade truce they agreed in October 2025 and to explore tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods on each side.

 

Denuclearization, end to Ukraine war?

Trump last met Putin, 74, in person in Alaska in August 2025. And the US leader said last month he wanted to hold a trilateral summit with Putin and Xi in China to discuss “denuclearization.”

He told reporters at the White House on October 20 that a three-way summit would be “a very positive thing for the world.”

Putin is alleged to have suggested the idea to Trump in a phone call on October 9, perhaps to broker an end to the war in Ukraine, without having Ukraine present for initial talks, according to sources that spoke to the Wall Street Journal.

Xi and Putin have, of course, met many times, including in May when the Russian leader visited Beijing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned last month that a trilateral summit could offer a platform to redistribute influence, similar to after World War II.

“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4’, with a redistribution of influence,” he said, referring to the 1945 summit of Soviet, US and British leaders on dividing up the post-war map.

“Russia wants this meeting more than anyone,” Zelensky said, warning against handing Moscow “another major diplomatic advantage”.

 

Ukraine honour for Melania

But US officials have just announced that US First Lady Melania Trump will host officials from Moscow and Kyiv at the White House on Thursday, ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war.

The talks have revived hopes for peace, as Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine grinds through its fifth year, and a recent rapprochement between Trump and Putin has raised concerns the US could turn its back on Kyiv.

Moscow’s adviser for international economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, and human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova plan to meet Melania Trump on Thursday “provided that all logistical arrangements work out”, Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency reported on Wednesday, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, announced he would also be meeting Melania Trump in Washington.

The meeting comes after Zelensky said he had “very detailed, hour-and-a-half-long” conversations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of next week’s meeting in Abu Dhabi, the first talks between all three sides since February.

Earlier on Wednesday, Zelensky awarded the first lady a national honour for her role in brokering a partial ceasefire that allowed the evacuation of civilians from a Russian-occupied town.

The text acknowledged her “significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine, and for active human rights and charitable work.”

Melania, who is expected to speak at 11am (1600 GMT) on Thursday, had announced a localized truce between Ukrainian and Russian forces last month to allow for residents of Oleshky on the southern front to leave after suffering weeks of shortages of food and medicine.

The rare halt in fighting, which was respected by both sides, allowed roads to be demined and residents to depart for either Ukraine or Russia.

She has also been involved in efforts to return Ukrainian children taken to Russia.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP

data.title: Chinese Stocks Rise; Dollar Down on Democrats’ Electoral Sweep
data.description:
The Chinese government’s intervention to rescue local stocks hammered by a prolonged ‘tech slump’ finally began to restore share values in Shanghai on Wednesday.

A $15-billion “barrage” of moves announced by the People’s Bank of China and financial regulators on Monday helped lift the CSI 300 index in Shanghai by up to 2%, although the gains were attributed to “state-backed investors,” according to the South China Morning Post.

Retail investors, it said, “refrained from bets on stocks this week, even after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.”

 

ALSO SEE: China Unveils Measures to Boost Markets after Big Falls in October

 

“Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30% in October, according to official data.

“The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up its efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply,” the paper said this afternoon.

“There is a difference between stopping the bleeding and restoring the patient to full health,” it quoted Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management, as saying.

“State-backed buying can steady the tape. Easier buy-back financing can improve liquidity. But if corporate earnings do not improve, the market eventually comes back to the same question. Who is buying once the government steps away?”

The CSI index had fallen for 12 consecutive weeks and stocks on China’s mainland had lost about $2.4 trillion in market value since May because investors had lost faith that Beijing’s AI boom would ever make a profit.

 

Study: Less disclosure to foreign investors

Another possible reason for the slump was a study published in The Accounting Review, which found that Chinese companies frequently provide less complete information to foreign investors than to domestic shareholders.

It said that English-language filings systematically offered less comprehensive information than their domestic Chinese counterparts, and that when researchers emailed Chinese companies posing as local versus foreign investors, the firms were half as likely to respond to the foreign inquiries.

The response gap worsened for companies with larger translation disparities in their public reports, according to the Wall Street Journal’s China correspondent.

Even native-Mandarin-speaking analysts at foreign brokerages suffered from a lack of direct communication, leading to less accurate earnings forecasts, the WSJ said, noting that selective disclosure reduces stock liquidity, and makes it harder and more expensive for these firms to raise capital.

 

Democratic sweep in US

Meanwhile, the big news of the day was the Democrat Party’s sweep of both Congress and the US Senate in the mid-term elections on Tuesday, which looks set to derail Donald Trump’s economic agenda as he heads into his final two years as president.

Equities and the dollar sank initially amid warnings that the result – which saw Republicans ousted in a so-called blue wave – could lead to gridlock on Capitol Hill after Trump warned that he would become “Mr Veto”.

Tech firms, already under pressure, were also hit by concerns about the future of data centre building – a major bone of contention in many places.

Tens of millions of Americans cast their vote in the crucial polls pitched as a referendum on the White House amid anger at surging petrol prices, tariffs and the Iran war.

With Democrats winning key races to flip the House and Senate – including once-safe Republican seats – Chris Weston at Pepperstone flagged “the potential for legislative gridlock, fiscal brinkmanship, debt-ceiling disputes, and congressional investigations,” AFP reported.

However, he added that “the president would retain considerable executive authority, so the implications for individual sectors are far from straightforward”.

Trump threatened in a telephone interview with the CBS network on Tuesday to be “Mr Veto” and block any Democratic legislation if they win.

The prospect of Congress coming to a standstill weighed on the dollar and Treasury yields, with observers pointing out that such a scenario would restrict spending.

Gold rose 2% after the vote, while cryptocurrencies dipped briefly amid concern over greater regulation on digital assets.

Bitcoin briefly hit a six-week low before recovering to trade close to flat by 0715 GMT at $78,070. Analysts say support has also been hit by the $6-billion hack of the Binance exchange late last week, which is the largest-ever crypto heist.

 

‘Poll could cut inflation, Treasury yields’

“Democratic control of Congress will make it harder for the White House administration to pass major partisan legislation. That could reduce the prospect of significant additional fiscal stimulus over the next two years,” wrote David Chao at Invesco.

“For Asia, the implications matter. Less fiscal stimulus could reduce upward pressure on US growth, inflation and Treasury yields, potentially easing some of the pressure that higher US rates and a stronger dollar have placed on Asian currencies and monetary policy.”

However, as the results came in, he offered a more conciliatory tone to the New York Times, saying he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and expected to work out deals with Democrats.

That provided the queue for a bounce in some stock markets, as well as the dollar and Treasury yields.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Seoul and reversed losses, while Mumbai, Bangkok, Wellington and Manila were also up.

However, Tokyo, Sydney, Taipei and Jakarta all fell.

London, Paris and Frankfurt opened with gains.

 

Doubt over AI buildout

While they managed to pare losses, tech firms remained under pressure as investors continue to fret over the AI investment boom and when firms that have pumped billions into the sector will eventually see returns, if ever.

Traders were also nervous about the outlook for the AI buildout, with many Democrats taking advantage of anger over data centre development.

“The concern isn’t that a Democratic governor automatically shuts the gates on data-centre construction,” said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

“It is that a change in political leadership could alter the regulatory environment just as developers are committing enormous amounts of capital to projects dependent on electricity availability and predictable construction schedules.”

However, Google was happy to announce plans on Wednesday to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years to build data centres and other digital infrastructure as demand for AI services booms in Asia.

The US tech giant said its data centre campuses in industrial zones would be “energy-efficient” while pledging to “bolster local water security, and add more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity” to Malaysia’s national grid.

 

Tech stocks slide, Iran says ‘no to war’

Meanwhile, Japanese chipmaker Kioxia plunged more than 5%, while Advantest and SoftBank lost more than 3%. Seoul’s SK Hynix and Samsung were also down.

Oil prices edged up as investors kept tabs on the Middle East after Trump confirmed US strikes on Iran but played down speculation he was preparing to resume bombing after the election.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” he told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday.

“I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

His Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was trying to resolve the crisis “through dialogue”, adding that “no one will benefit from this war” if it reignited.

However, Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Islamic republic was “ready for battle with its finger on the trigger”, while Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tehran retained the right to “legitimate self-defence”.

He later posted on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message”.

data.title: China Unveils Measures to Boost Markets after Big Falls in October
data.description:
Authorities in China announced a range of measures on Monday to bolster local equity markets, which suffered severe declines in October.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) unveiled a 100-billion-yuan ($15 billion) asset swap facility with 31 securities firms, plus asset management companies and insurers. That is a one-year arrangement which is due to start on Tuesday.

The central bank also said it would increase the number of institutions that can participate in the scheme and introduce a small cut to reduce swap fees.

 

ALSO SEE: Cambodian Regime Seen Deeply Involved in Scam Centres: Amnesty

 

The central bank will reduce the interest rate – from 1.25% to 1% – on a special relending program to support share buybacks and help major shareholders increase equity stakes, it said.

It has urged commercial banks to scale up lending and said the policy to do that will be permanent, the South China Morning Post said.

Officials with the PBOC met with their counterparts from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) and other regulators today in a bid to stabilize local markets and show they would defend equity markets after the sell-off last month that rocked investors.

Institutional investors will be able to trade illiquid assets with the central bank to be able to buy stocks, the paper said.

Meanwhile, the CSRC plans to expand the scope of relending and support tools to encourage more tech companies to participate and attract major index constituents.

Regulators will also ease restrictions on leveraged trading and indicated that state-linked investors, often known as the “national team”, which help counter sell-offs in tech and AI-related equities.

The CSI 300 index, which tracks the largest companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen, slumped by 8.5% last month. It became a bear market on October 20, after a 20% drop, and had fallen for 12 consecutive weeks.

The Star 50 index in Shanghai, dominated by large chip and tech firms, has been one of the worst hit. It has plunged by about 40% in less than four months, and seen share losses of about $480 billion.

Stocks on China’s mainland have lost about $2.4 trillion in market value since May, according to Yahoo Finance, which said last week that investors had lost faith that Beijing’s AI boom would ever make a profit.

Goldman Sachs says AI companies have about 42% of the market value of Chinese shares listed on the mainland and in Hong Kong, over half of current of trading, which means when they fall, they drag the local markets down with them.

The main problem appears to be doubt that AI companies and other tech firms, such as those making robots, will ever earn back the money spent on their products.

News of Beijing’s intent to support local markets helped lift Shanghai by 1.08% on Monday, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong was also up 0.42%.

 

Oil prices fall

Meanwhile, in other business news, oil prices fell about 6% on Monday because of the flurry of talks going on to try to end the war in the Middle East. Brent crude was just over $106 a barrel, while WTI was at $97.45.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that “very intensive” talks are underway with the United States via mediators, amid fears that the war might reignite after the US mid-term elections this week.

“Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive. Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active mediating role in these negotiations,” he said in a video interview given to the official IRNA news agency.

China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing.

The meetings come days after US President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict, which was triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran and has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.

Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security”, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.

Wang later called for dialogue to end the conflict “while safeguarding regional energy security and the safety of shipping lanes”, as he met with Saudi National Security Adviser Musaad bin Mohammad al-Aiban.

China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict that has disrupted global shipping.

Trump said on Saturday that the United States had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, with Tehran warning of reprisals if attacked.

“All parties should… in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement.

data.title: Cambodian Regime Seen Deeply Involved in Scam Centres: Amnesty
data.description:
The involvement of state officials – police and military officers – in the operation of many scam compounds in Cambodia suggests the regime is still deeply involved in the “sickening” and highly abusive industry, according to Amnesty International.

Agnes Callamard, secretary-general of the international human rights body, addressed a packed press conference in Bangkok on Thursday, saying extensive investigative research in recent months had identified five security companies guarding 23 of the 86 scam compounds in the country.

The group said evidence had been found showing that Cambodian military and police worked at many of the scam compounds it visited over the past two years, where trafficking victims were forced to work – and were allegedly beaten, raped, and given electric shocks if they failed to meet quota targets.

 

ALSO SEE: Nickel Sold in London ‘Linked to Rainforest Depletion in Indonesia’

 

Callamard said the group’s latest report, titled ‘Official Business: Security Companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia‘, “reads like a sadistic horror movie.”

 

‘Corporate actors, crimes against humanity’

The allegations linked to scam centres violated both international and domestic laws and may amount to crimes against humanity.

She warned that “corporate actors” such as owners, directors, managers, as well as individual guards, “may be deemed responsible,” the French rights activist said.

“The fingerprint of the Cambodian state is everywhere,” she alleged, saying that while the country had conducted a crackdown that shut down many scam centres around the country, the “government’s crackdowns were woefully inadequate.”

“They didn’t properly investigate the persons involved and took no action against the security companies” working at the compounds.

The security companies were part of the “architecture that allows those compounds to exist,” she said, adding that the role of private security firms should be investigated because it was a “sickening criminal racket”.

Callamard acknowledged that scam compounds were now transnational activities that often involved Chinese and local criminal networks, but said Cambodian authorities “failed to hold anyone to account.”

Amnesty documented private security guards operating at all the 82 compounds it visited since 2024, “with survivors consistently describing compounds staffed by dozens, and sometimes hundreds, of guards who enforced confinement, prevented escape, responded to resistance and, in many cases, directly participated in torture and other serious abuses.”

Researchers from the rights group visited 82 of the 86 scamming compounds it identified in earlier reports last year and in June. They took photos of guards, which revealed their company’s logos and uniforms. These were then shown to 151 survivors interviewed over the past three years.

 

‘Evidence on social media’

“Geolocations of videos posted by 222 social media accounts that were confirmed to belong to guards or showed guards working at scamming compounds,” the report said, noting that it reviewed more than 25,000 videos and photos from these accounts in recent months.

It also reviewed documents published by the companies or their staff, such as corporate records filed with the Ministry of Commerce, employment ads posted on Telegram, Facebook and TikTok over the past 18 months. That showed individuals who were current or former members of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces or National Police.

It names five of the companies, which it said worked to hide their identity. One was linked to a senior national police official.

The Amnesty report documents torture and punishment of people who tried to escape, resisted orders, or failed to meet work standards. A Ugandan man alleged that guards at a facility known as PV01 (or Park 8) beat him and shocked him with electric batons while his hands were chained to a pole above a water basin.

A Ugandan woman alleged being repeatedly raped by her boss, while a Kenyan man described guards coming regularly “to beat detainees on the orders of compound managers”, it said.

So many Africans have been caught up in the scam compounds in Cambodia and neighbouring countries that Callamard said she plans to visit Kenya soon to publicize the risk of people flying to the ASEAN region for “fake jobs” that could destroy people’s lives.

None of the latest allegations are a surprise, given general recognition that crime networks have been making vast amounts of money. Scam compounds in Southeast Asia were estimated to have reaped $64 billion in 2023.

Analysts and researchers monitoring developments in both Cambodia and Myawaddy – an enclave in southeast Myanmar near the Thai border controlled by a Karen militia aligned with the military junta, where huge compounds have been demolished – have consistently said these moves were simply stunts to try to minimize punitive responses by the US, China and global monitors such as the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

Cambodia became a major hub for online scamming after the Covid-19 pandemic. The multi-billion-dollar industry evolved from illegal gambling and relied heavily on people lured from dozens of countries around the world by fraudulent job ads, who were subject to coercion, violence and exploitation after flying to Southeast Asia.

 

Amnesty said these activities were embedded in legitimate business structures such as licensed casinos and hotels in special economic zones, until the violent and scandalous nature of these activities were revealed over the past two years.

Analysts such as Jason Tower, now with the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, and Harvard University researcher Jacob Sims, revealed the dramatic expansion by Chinese crime gangs in Myanmar, northern Laos and Cambodia.

In January 2025, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said Huione Group, a Cambodian company with ties to the country’s ruling family, was “the largest online criminal marketplace in history.” It reportedly had $24 billion in funds traced through Huione Guarantee over the previous 3.5 years.

A report by Sims in May last year said transnational fraud was “perhaps the most dominant economic activity in the entire Mekong subregion – equivalent to nearly half of total GDP (gross domestic product) in the primary host countries” – Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

This led to the US and UK imposing sanctions on Prince Group founder Chen Zhi and the seizure of a vast haul of bitcoin, plus assets worth $700m in October last year. Then, in January, the alleged ‘scam billionaire’ was arrested and flown to China.

These actions by China, the US, plus ASEAN neighbours and major donors such as Japan, spurred a major crackdown by the Hun Manet government that saw thousands arrested and hundreds of people deported. However, Amnesty said its response caused a humanitarian crisis, because “thousands of traumatised survivors were left to fend for themselves with no state support.”

Callamard said if governments want to stage raids at such facilities, “you have to prepare for the consequences.” And “a crackdown won’t work till you get to the root of the problem.”

She said governments need to change the way victims are treated.

“It is a web of deceit, a web of violence. Multilateral cooperation is absolutely crucial, otherwise it’s never going to stop.”

Amnesty rejected any suggestion that their press conference had been discussed with the Thai government, which is involved in bitter wrangling with Phnom Penh after two short bursts of conflict over their bilateral border last year.

Meanwhile, Thai officials are watching both Cambodia and Myanmar’s response to international calls for scam compounds to be shut down. They are well aware that crime gangs previously based in Myawaddy have dispersed – either shifted abroad or moved to more discreet sites north, south or west of the border enclave.

More than 50 sites – many targeting the US – are still believed to be operating in Myanmar. Indeed, local analysts say scam centres are about the only places in the Karen borderlands not getting bombed by the Myanmar airforce in the civil war that has raged on multiple fronts since the 2021 coup.

 

  • Jim Pollard

data.title: Jio Surges 21% in Indian IPO, Raises $3 Billion in Record Debut
data.description:
Jio Platforms enjoyed a record market debut on the National Stock Exchange on Wednesday, raising over $3 billion in India’s biggest ever initial public offering.

Shares of the country’s biggest wireless operator opened at 1,358 rupees, which was 21% up on its 1,119-rupee issue price.

Jio is the digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Launched a decade ago, Jio’s wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

 

ALSO SEE: Anthropic Admits AI Risks in IPO Filing; Australia’s Cyber Warning

 

With more than 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into newer areas such as digital services and artificial intelligence.

The listing, one of the most anticipated this year, attracted robust demand last week with the IPO being 22 times oversubscribed.

“In our first 10 years, we democratised data… In our next 10, we want to democratise every technology that can transform Indian lives,” Akash Ambani, managing director of Jio Platforms and Mukesh’s eldest son, said at the listing ceremony in financial capital Mumbai.

“AI, cloud, connected devices, connectivity even from space and digital services not yet imagined.”

Analysts at Nomura, who initiated coverage on the stock on Wednesday, said the company’s focus for Jio had shifted “from adding users to earning more from each customer”.

“We believe the heavy 5G investment cycle is largely behind for Jio… freeing up significant cash flow,” they said.

Experts say Jio is key to Reliance’s strategy to evolve beyond its traditional oil business and the touchstone of its future tech ambitions.

Local media have reported that it is considering a low-orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space – a venture that would see it compete with Elon Musk’s Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.

The world’s richest man accused unnamed Indian “oligarchs” this month of preventing Starlink’s rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance chairman as “Prime Minister Ambani” and the “real boss of India”.

Reliance responded by noting that it had never “feared competition” and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink.

While Jio has expanded beyond its telecom roots, experts have cautioned investors that it will take time for its efforts to bear fruit.

 

SK Hynix lifts tech stocks

Meanwhiile, technology firms surged in Asia on Wednesday after blockbuster earnings from chip giant SK Hynix helped boost optimism in the AI trade ahead of results from Wall Street titans Microsoft and Alphabet.

Oil prices rose as investors kept tabs on Israel’s election results, which could determine the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s war against Iran.

After a slight wobble this month in the tech realm caused by fresh worries about huge investment spending, profitability and company finances, AI-linked firms were back on the front foot.

SK Hynix, which has been at the forefront of the chip boom, said Wednesday that third-quarter operating profit soared 632% to $62.8 billion thanks to explosive demand for its advanced semiconductors.

The firm said it had now posted record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

“While Wall Street argues over whether the AI arms race can keep financing itself, SK Hynix has just reminded the market that somebody on the other side of all that capex is receiving the cheque,” wrote Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

The reading added to optimism surrounding the sector after Anthropic, the mother company for Claude AI, said on Monday in its IPO filing that first-half revenue surged about 1,300% and flagged heavy capital spending ahead.

That was followed on Tuesday by Broadcom’s announcing jointly with Citi, Blackstone and Morgan Stanley a $63 billion financing structure to build new capacity for Anthropic.

“The AI trade has undoubtedly received a healthy shot in the arm from Anthropic’s… filing, with its incredible revenue growth, improving compute economics and substantial commitments to future infrastructure investment reinforcing the longer-term opportunity across the AI supply chain,” Pepperstone’s Chris Weston said.

Shares in SK Hynix soared almost 11% on Wednesday and South Korean rival Samsung, which reports Thursday, added 9%. That pushed Seoul’s Kospi index up more than 6%.

 

Asian markets mixed

Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed more than 1%, with chipmaker Kioxia soaring 13.8%, while Advantest gained more than 3% and Tokyo Electron 4.4%.

Taipei was pulled sharply higher thanks to chipmaker TSMC’s strong performance, while Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore and Wellington were also well up.

Still, Sydney was flat, while Manila and Bangkok also dipped. Mumbai fell despite Jio’s record $3-billion IPO.

The gains tracked advances in New York, where the Nasdaq added more than 1%. Microsoft and Alphabet are due to report later in the day, while Amazon, Apple and Intel follow on Thursday.

However, traders are also awaiting the Federal Reserve’s policy decision on Wednesday.

While it is expected to stand pat after last month’s hike, its post-meeting statement and comments from boss Kevin Warsh will be pored over for clues about its future plans. Markets expect a hike in December.

Crude prices jumped more than 2% as results from Israel’s general election rolled in.

While polls appeared to show Netanyahu’s governing Likud and the opposition neck and neck, the prime minister vowed to form a new coalition, adding that he could work with US President Donald Trump to eliminate the “existential threat” posed by Iran.

His comments came after opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said the country had chosen change and that he would seek to form a new administration.

data.title: Anthropic Admits AI Risks in IPO Filing; Australia’s Cyber Warning
data.description:
Anthropic, one of the world’s top artificial intelligence companies, has unveiled its plan to list on the stock market – with news of booming sales, but also long and extraordinary admissions on potentially dire safety risks.

The move in the US on Monday occurs amid uncertainty around the globe on whether the AI boom can deliver profits. However, some appear to believe the huge listing next month will help both the firm and the sector.

But it comes at a time when people around the world now regard AI as a greater threat than climate change, a new study by French insurer Axa found.

 

ALSO SEE: Thailand in $1.5bn Solar Power Push; CCP Meets in Beijing

 

Indeed, Australia’s cybersecurity agency warned on Tuesday that artificial intelligence poses an “unprecedented” threat because foreign governments could use it to hack computer networks and critical infrastructure.

Anthropic’s filing warns investors of dangers ranging from conflict with the Trump administration to AI systems acting on their own, alongside huge spending commitments on computing power.

The listing would be the first by one of the standalone companies leading the race to build advanced AI, ahead of its main rival OpenAI, the ChatGPT-maker, which has pushed back its own market debut to next year.

It also follows the June listing of SpaceX, which owns Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI and saw its shares fall sharply after a strong debut.

A disappointing reception for Anthropic could dent investor enthusiasm for AI, a sector that has become a key driver of the US economy amid worries of a market bubble.

According to The Wall Street Journal, the company is aiming to go public the week of November 16, though the timing could change.

 

90 pages of prospectus devoted to risks

The offering could raise as much as $100 billion in an initial public offering (IPO) that could value Anthropic at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, the Wall Street Journal added, citing people familiar with the matter.

The 400-page prospectus devotes over 90 pages to risks specific to an industry that has faced a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.

It also reflects the dominant belief among researchers inside Anthropic that AI needs to be developed by a safe pair of hands, or otherwise see its extraordinary powers misused, with China having the edge.

The filing cited concerns that advanced systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”

Anthropic also warned that its “engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action.”

The company has been targeted in recent months by the administration of US President Donald Trump for refusing to lift restrictions on how the Pentagon could use its technology, and the Defense Department has since labeled it a national security risk and barred it as a supplier.

Despite these challenges, Anthropic’s business has grown very quickly. Sales reached $11.6 billion in the April-June quarter, up from $787 million a year earlier. That compares with $4.6 billion in sales for all of 2025.

The company made its first operating profit in that quarter, close to $1 billion. It still reported an overall loss of $80 billion for the first half of the year, mostly because of accounting charges linked to its rising value rather than cash spent.

Much of the growth comes from businesses using Claude to write software and handle office work. Nearly 12,000 organizations now spend at least $100,000 a year with Anthropic, up from fewer than 1,000 a year ago.

 

Huge spending on computing capacity

Anthropic warned that its growth is likely to slow, possibly sharply, and investors will be closely looking at the company’s third-quarter figures that will be released before the IPO.

To power its AI, Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity, including up to $120.5 billion with SpaceX, about $110 billion with Amazon and an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion with Google.

It has also signed an agreement to use a $32-billion data centre in outback Australia.

The company warned that if demand falls short of its projections, many of these payments must be made regardless of how much capacity it actually uses.

The company will have a governance structure that gives power to its founders and not investors.

The company’s seven co-founders, led by Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his sister, company President Daniela Amodei, will keep control of just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, meaning outside investors will not be able to outvote them.

Anthropic is registered as a “public benefit corporation,” which requires it to weigh its goal of developing AI safely alongside making money for shareholders.

The co-founders have each pledged to give 80 percent of their shares to charity, though the filing notes these pledges are not legally binding.

 

Concern over hackers using AI

Meanwhile, the Australian Signals Directorate said on Tuesday that rapidly advancing AI models could be of huge benefit if harnessed for good, even using some AI tools to compile its own annual “cyber threat” report.

But recent months had also shown how AI was helping criminals and state-sponsored hackers launch attacks at “greater scale than ever before”, the directorate said in the report.

“AI has been the defining force in the cyber threat landscape over the past year, allowing malicious actors to find vulnerabilities faster and exploit them at unprecedented scale, speed and sophistication,” the report read.

“In recent weeks, new threats have emerged from the unintended actions of AI agents and model testing.”

Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from leading developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

The report documented a stark increase in cybersecurity incidents. The ASD issued more than 4,400 warnings about potentially malicious activity over the past year – an 80% increase compared to the prior 12 months.

“State-sponsored cyber actors continued to target Australian organisations primarily to gain access to sensitive or non-public information.

“This activity extends beyond government networks, and includes critical infrastructure entities, private businesses and individuals.”

The report said hackers linked to China, Russia and North Korea had targeted Australia or its allies in recent times.

Defence Minister Richard Marles said the nation could not ignore the AI revolution.

“AI is here and it’s real. People need to engage,” he told reporters. “There’s no turning the clock back in relation to that. Malicious actors are using AI to find vulnerabilities in systems.”

Marles urged Australians to update their computers and “harden their systems”.

Governments and firms have in recent days been rushing to fix critical flaws in a programming language that runs a large share of the world’s websites.

The vulnerability was found using a powerful model from OpenAI.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP.

data.title: Thailand in $1.5bn Solar Power Push; CCP Meets in Beijing
data.description:
Thailand is ramping up its transition from fossil fuels to renewables. The Anutin Charnvirakul government offered subsidies worth up to $1.5 billion on Monday to help a million households install solar panels.

It is offering a subsidy of 50,000 baht (close to $1,500) to homeowners to help with installation costs in a move that aims to reduce dependence on costly imports of gas.

It is also promising low-interest loans and tax benefits for those fitting panels to their homes or land.

 

ALSO SEE: Oil Near Five-Month High, Typhoon Champi Shuts Down Taiwan

 

“Today, we import a lot of our energy, we’re among the top buyers globally,” Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas told reporters. But he said this “was not a sustainable solution”.

The solar panel subsidy is expected to be approved at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday (Oct 27), with applications to open soon after, Ekniti said.

It will be funded out of a 400-billion-baht emergency borrowing package announced earlier this year to cushion the economic impacts of the Middle East war.

Around 60% of electricity production in Thailand comes from natural gas, with renewables currently only making up about 11%, according to government data from January to July 2026.

Much of the gas has historically come from offshore production or via pipeline from Myanmar, but declining production has forced Bangkok to step up liquid natural gas (LNG) imports.

Imported LNG made up 32% of its natural gas in the January-July period. Qatar was a major supplier but its gas infrastructure has been hit by the US and Israeli war with Iran, as has energy production across the region.

Thailand aims to have 51% of domestic electricity generated from renewable sources by 2037, AFP reported.

 

Xi aiming for 4th term

China’s President Xi Jinping opened a key meeting of Communist Party elites in Beijing on Monday, state media said, which observers will be closely watching for clues on the country’s direction and future leadership.

Roughly 300 members of the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee in attendance at the meeting, called the fifth plenum, will be looking to tighten discipline within their ranks, according to state media.

That includes measures to reduce corruption and make cadres more effective and loyal.

Xi opened the session on Monday, presenting a draft decision by the Central Committee that “sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance”, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Few details from the closed-door gathering, held under tight security, will be made known until it concludes on Thursday, but the timing of the meeting is crucial.

The fifth plenum comes ahead of a major party congress next year, where 73-year-old Xi is almost certain to secure a historic fourth term and oversee a leadership reshuffle. Previous plenums have represented key moments for Xi to cement his authority.

 

Thousands purged

The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has purged thousands of officials, including dozens of the Central Committee. Yet he remains frustrated with cadres he deems are not implementing his orders.

State media published an article ahead of the plenum, based on a speech Xi gave in January in which he railed against “two-faced” officials who appear to comply with central directives but “inwardly resist”, pursue “individualism” and are “politically opportunistic”.

Analysts told AFP that Xi is trying to maximise efficiency and loyalty among cadres by imposing more supervision and rules.

But as a result of his expansive purges, this year’s plenum is expected to have the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong’s death in 1976.

Eight of the Central Committee’s seats lie vacant, with another 15 members under investigation and at risk of being replaced.

Xi’s anti-corruption drive has also targeted the military, toppling five of the seven members of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the party’s top armed forces body.

Of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022, only two have not been purged or disappeared, according to the Asia Society Policy Institute.

The plenum could see new members appointed to the CMC; the party could wait until next year’s congress to replenish it; or Xi might even restructure party control over its vast military.

The talks also come at an unsteady time for the world’s second-largest economy, which has struggled to address persistently sluggish domestic spending and a protracted crisis in the crucial property sector.

Turbulent political and economic ties with the United States are also weighing on China’s leaders.

Authorities are expected to release a summary of the outcomes after the meeting concludes on Thursday.

 

Stocks mostly rise before tech earnings, central bank calls

Meanwhile, the world’s main stock markets mostly climbed on Monday as investors geared up for the week’s crucial run of central bank decisions and tech earnings, while oil prices retreated from a six-month high.

“The AI complex remains under a microscope ahead of what may be the most important stretch of earnings season so far,” noted SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are about to walk on stage, and this is not one of those quarters where a company can simply beat the number, raise the guidance by a whisker and expect applause. Investors want proof now.

“They want to know whether the billions going into the compute buildout are building a durable earnings machine or just a shinier version of the same old capex furnace,” Innes added.

This week also sees the release of earnings from South Korean chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung. Results from Tesla and Meta last week stoked spending worries that weighed on stock markets.

Wall Street ended in the red on Friday, and Asia followed suit at the open on Monday, although some staged a recovery.

Europe’s main stock markets were higher in late morning deals. Oil prices dropped moderately following Friday’s surge of more than 3% fuelled by supply concerns heading into the northern hemisphere winter.

 

Interest rate calls

Also in view this week are monetary policy decisions from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of Japan (BoJ).

While the Fed is expected to hold borrowing costs on Wednesday, traders will be keen to get an insight into its thinking following last month’s hike and as inflation remains well above its two percent target.

France’s deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the ECB meets on Thursday, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone’s second-biggest economy just yet.

The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having hiked twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the US-Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.

The BoJ is also forecast to sit tight this month, while the Bank of England is widely expected to hike in November after a jump for UK inflation ahead of the country’s annual budget announcement due Wednesday.

data.title: Oil Near Five-Month High, Typhoon Champi Shuts Down Taiwan
data.description:
Oil traded at a five-month high on Friday, with the benchmark Brent North Sea crude close to $115 a barrel, boosted by speculation of further US and Israeli attacks after the US mid-term voting.

Asian markets closed the week mixed, with tech firms able to claw back some of the week’s hefty losses, while stock markets mostly dropped in Europe.

Key developments in Asia were the arrival of typhoon Champi, the 30th typhoon of the year, which shut down Taiwan and is being closely watched in Japan because it was heading in a northwesterly direction (more on that below).

 

ALSO SEE: Rush to Fix Websites’ Security Flaw; China Tax on Offshore Wealth

 

Stock prices of AI-linked companies have been pummelled by concerns in recent months of being overvalued and that their huge outlays on infrastructure and hardware might not return a profit. Plus, recently, their servicing costs have been spiralling.

That concern has combined with an Iran war-fuelled surge in oil prices to more than $100 that has ramped up inflation, forced central banks to hike interest rates and sent government borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

Strong earnings in past quarters have been able to temper many of the concerns, but analysts pointed out that investors are demanding better and better results to justify their backing.

Earnings from Facebook-parent Meta and chip equipment maker Lam Research this week have beaten forecasts but seen their shares dive.

“Even positive news is being ignored,” FOREX.com’s Fawad Razaqzada said. “Strong results are no longer enough if the outlook fails to match an already demanding valuation. Investors are becoming much less forgiving.”

The rush out of tech has, however, boosted industrial companies overlooked for much of the AI boom, with the Dow rising this week while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 retreated.

The general losses in New York filtered through to Asia in the morning, but some markets staged a comeback as the day progressed.

Seoul – which was at the forefront of the AI boom and has led recent losses – shed more than 2% after the open but was up at the close.

Chipmaker and market heavyweight SK Hynix – a major target amid the waves of buying and selling – ended up more than 4%. That rise came after its US shares fell more than 8% on Thursday after saying it was scrapping plans for an initial public offering for its US subsidiary Solidigm, citing “market conditions and share price trends”.

There were also gains on Friday in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Jakarta.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225, which is also heavily weighted to tech, ended in the red, though well off earlier lows. Wellington, Mumbai and Manila were also down. Taipei was closed as Typhoon Champi neared Taiwan.

London, Frankfurt and Paris dropped in the morning. Safe havens benefited, with the yen rallying against the dollar, helped by strong Japanese inflation data that boosted bets on another interest rate hike.

The currency has struggled against the greenback in recent years owing to the wide interest rate gap between the United States and Japan, as well as worries about the Asian giant’s fiscal situation.

 

Taiwan battens down

Most shops and schools were shut across Taiwan on Friday as Typhoon Champi neared the island, forcing hundreds of people to leave their homes ahead of the powerful storm.

The typhoon is expected to sweep past Taiwan’s northeast as it moves towards China and Japan, triggering the cancellation of hundreds of flights in the region.

At least one person was killed in Taiwan after being swept away by waves whipped up by the typhoon, authorities said. Dozens of others have been injured.

Champi is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbo-charged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.

The storm was briefly a super typhoon as it crossed the ocean, but has been weakening as it approaches Taiwan and now has maximum sustained wind speeds of 167 kilometres (104 miles) per hour, according to the latest update from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

Heavy rain, strong winds and giant waves are forecast for Friday and Saturday, and thousands of military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts.

More than 1,200 people had been evacuated from their homes ahead of Champi.

“As it approaches Taiwan’s northeastern tip… the typhoon may slow down. If it slows down, its impact will last longer,” the Central Weather Administration’s Lu Kuo-chen told a briefing.

 

‘Extremely heavy rain’

Champi is expected to dump up to 90 centimetres (35 inches) of rain from Thursday to Saturday, with northeastern Taiwan to be hardest hit, the forecaster said.

“People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow,” Lu said.

Work and classes were cancelled for the day across nearly all of Taiwan, leaving streets quiet as most locals hunkered down at home. The stock exchange was also closed.

Some businesses installed sandbags or metal barriers at entrances to prevent flooding.

The United Nations said Wednesday that the El Nino system gripping the planet is heading off the charts, and that countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.

El Nino is expected to peak in December, but the human impact is set to last into 2027 and beyond.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate human-caused global warming.

 

Micron wage talks suspended

Hundreds of workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taiwan have rejected the US memory chip giant’s proposal for a new profit-sharing system, the union representing the employees said Friday, declaring the “struggle is far from over”.

Exploding global demand for chips used in AI data centres has sent revenues soaring for firms like Micron, but as their earnings skyrocket, workers are calling for a bigger cut of profits.

Micron, which makes around 50-60% of its chips in Taiwan, has spent weeks in talks over remuneration with two labour unions representing 12,000 of 15,000 workers at its Taoyuan and Taichung plants.

The company and the union representing workers at its larger plant in Taichung struck an agreement on Wednesday, but the Taoyuan union is still locked in negotiations with management and held a small strike on Thursday to press their point.

Around 70% of the Taoyuan union’s more than 2,300 members voted to reject the company’s profit-sharing proposal presented to them on Thursday, the union said in a statement.

“During negotiations with Micron on October 21, the company failed to respond to any of the union’s demands,” the union said, warning of potential “further collective action to secure a fairer profit-sharing system”.

“In addition, we have continued to receive reports of dissatisfaction with the company’s proposal from rank-and-file Micron employees in Taichung,” it added.

Micron Taiwan said in a statement on Friday it will “continue discussions with the Taoyuan union on October 27 in a spirit of mutual respect and good faith”.

It said it “remains committed to listening to their perspectives and concerns, fostering mutual understanding and trust through open and candid communication”.

The US company’s share price has ballooned more than 300% over the past year, as it reports record earnings fuelled by AI demand.

Micron Taiwan chairman Lu Donghui said on Thursday the company had agreed to introduce a quarterly profit-sharing bonus system starting in fiscal 2027 for its global workforce, in addition to the existing annual bonus.

For workers in Taiwan, the company will increase pension contribution and shift allowances, among other measures, Lu said.

The Micron dispute follows labour disagreements in Korea, where Samsung Electronics averted a strike by agreeing to a deal to distribute bonuses equivalent to 10.5% of operating profit to its semiconductor employees.

data.title: Hackers in $6bn Hit on Binance Exchange; North Korea Suspected
data.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Friday it was battling to resolve a “complex attack” by hackers that resulted in the theft of about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets.

The company said it coordinated with industry partners, such as stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, to freeze roughly $3 billion of the stolen funds before they could be laundered or cashed out.

Blockchain intelligence firms such as TRM Labs and Chainalysis have said they believe the attack – the biggest ever to date – was undertaken by TraderTraitor, which is a state-sponsored North Korean hacking unit, reportedly linked to the Lazarus Group.

 

ALSO SEE: Cambodian Regime Seen Deeply Involved in Scam Centres: Amnesty

 

Binance said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach”, contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.

“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.

The firm earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”

The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion,” AFP reported.

That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.

Binance warned the figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”

The 2025 Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.

Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said on Thursday it had “high confidence” that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing “robust on and off-chain intelligence.”

“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for “The Interview,” a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

 

Deposits not affected

At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended”.

“Deposits remain unaffected,” it said.

The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorized party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.

But it said later that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.”

Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether – a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT – said his firm froze about $1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”

Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.

USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.

The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

 

Crypto prices tumble

For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.

The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.

Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly 5% and nearly 6%, respectively, on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

 

  • AFP with additional editing and input by Jim Pollard
